passage: Ines stood on a small stool at the low table in Lisbon, her tongue between her teeth. She had a damp cloth and a serious face. Esther, her mother, sat with her tea and did not move. Ines wiped in big circles, and water ran over the edge onto the floor. She missed the crumbs near the edge. "Done!" she said. Esther looked at the wet table and the drip on the floor. She said, "Thank you, Ines, that helps. Shall we do the corner together?" Ines beamed and pushed the cloth over the last crumbs. Then she stood back and said proudly, "I am a helper."

qa.q: What did Ines use to wipe the table?
qa.a: Ines used a damp cloth.

qa.q: How did Ines feel when she said "Done!"?
qa.a: Ines felt proud and important, even though the table was still wet and had crumbs.

qa.q: What did Esther do that made Ines want to keep helping?
qa.a: Esther thanked Ines, did not take the cloth away and offered to do the corner together.

qa.q: What might Esther be thinking as she looks at the wet table?
qa.a: Esther can see it is messy, but she is patient and values Ines feeling useful more than a perfect table.

grounding: Shows a young child proudly wiping a table slowly and messily, and a parent patiently accepting the imperfect help.

passage: At snack time, Irawati, the nursery teacher, handed out the paper plates. "Who wants to be plate helper today?" Vasudha's hand shot up. She carried one plate at a time from the pile to each friend, slowly, with both hands, her lips pressed together. The third plate slipped and clattered on the mat. Vasudha froze and looked up. Irawati smiled. "Plates fall. Pick it up and carry on." Vasudha picked it up. When all the plates were down, she stood at the front, chest out. "I did the plates," she said. Irawati gave her a small sticker of a star.

qa.q: Who was the plate helper at snack time?
qa.a: Vasudha was the plate helper at snack time.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when the plate clattered on the mat?
qa.a: Vasudha was startled and worried about being in trouble, which is why she froze and looked up.

qa.q: What did Irawati do that helped Vasudha keep trying?
qa.a: Irawati smiled, said plates fall and asked Vasudha to pick it up and carry on.

qa.q: How might the other children feel as Vasudha hands out the plates?
qa.a: The other children probably feel pleased to be served by a friend, and may want a turn as plate helper.

grounding: Shows a young child carrying plates slowly and clumsily, with a teacher accepting imperfect help and building confidence.

passage:
Uma: "Mumma, can I stir the kheer?"
Jasleen: "Yes, but slowly. Hold the handle, not the pot."
Uma: (stirring hard) "Like this?"
Jasleen: "A bit slower, beta. It's splashing."
Uma: "Oops. Some fell on the floor."
Jasleen: "That's okay. We'll wipe it after."
Uma: "Can I wipe it? I'm a good wiper."
Jasleen: "You are. Here's the cloth."
(Uma wipes the floor, leaving a wide sticky streak.)
Uma: "All clean!"
Jasleen: (smiling, wiping the streak later) "Thank you, my helper."
Uma: "Tomorrow can I carry the plates?"
Jasleen: "The steel ones, yes. One at a time."

qa.q: What was Uma stirring?
qa.a: Uma was stirring the kheer.

qa.q: How did Uma feel about helping in the kitchen?
qa.a: She felt proud and eager, calling herself a good wiper and asking to carry plates tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do well in accepting Uma's messy help?
qa.a: She let Uma stir and wipe, praised her, gave simple safety tips and quietly finished the streak later without taking over.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel about the extra mess?
qa.a: Jasleen seems patient and warm, smiling and accepting that the imperfect help matters more than a spotless floor.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young child proudly helping in the kitchen, messily, and a parent patiently accepting the imperfect help.

passage:
Nursery teacher's note, Monday.
Today Sahil, five, asked if he could set out the plates for snack time. He carried them one by one from the shelf, very seriously, tongue between his teeth. It took him nearly ten minutes, twice as long as usual. One plate went on the floor; he picked it up and put it back on the table, and I swapped it for a clean one without fuss. When everyone sat down, he announced, "I did the plates!" and beamed. I thanked him in front of the class. I will give him the same job all this week, and let him choose a helper on Friday.
Vinita

qa.q: How long did Sahil take to set out the plates?
qa.a: It took him nearly ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when everyone sat down?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, beaming as he announced that he did the plates.

qa.q: Why was Vinita right to let Sahil keep the job?
qa.a: Patiently accepting his slow, imperfect help lets him feel useful, which builds confidence more than doing it for him.

qa.q: How might the other children see Sahil's job?
qa.a: They might feel curious and want a turn, seeing how proud Sahil is and knowing he can choose a helper on Friday.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child proudly setting out plates slowly and imperfectly, and an adult accepting the help.

passage: In their village near Mysuru, Devika, four, followed her grandfather Harsha to the cowshed every morning. Today she wanted to carry the small bucket of water. It sloshed with every step, and half spilled on her feet. She giggled. When they reached the cow, there was only a little water left. Dada didn't take the bucket. He held it steady while she poured it into the trough. "Good job, kutti." Then she tried to sweep the straw with his broom, which was taller than her. Straw went everywhere. Dada swept it again later without a word. At breakfast, Devika told Amma, "I fed the cow," puffing her chest out.

qa.q: What did Devika want to carry?
qa.a: She wanted to carry the small bucket of water.

qa.q: How did Devika feel at breakfast?
qa.a: She felt proud, puffing her chest out as she told Amma she fed the cow.

qa.q: What did Dada do that helped Devika grow?
qa.a: He let her carry and pour, praised her, and quietly swept again later instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Amma feel hearing Devika's news?
qa.a: Amma would likely feel warm and amused, happy to see how proud Devika is of helping.

grounding: Shows a young child helping with farm chores slowly and messily, and a grandparent patiently accepting the imperfect help.

passage: Marek pushed the stool to the kitchen sink in their Kraków flat. "I wash the potatoes!" His dad, Alejandro, handed him the brush and five muddy potatoes. Marek scrubbed each one very hard, tongue poking out. Water splashed on the floor and on the cat. One potato was still brown on one side. Alejandro's hand moved towards it, then stopped. "Good scrubbing. That one has a muddy spot. Can you find it?" Marek turned it round, found the spot and scrubbed again. "All clean!" he shouted, holding it up like a prize. At dinner Marek told everyone, "I made the soup."

qa.q: How many potatoes did Alejandro give Marek?
qa.a: Five muddy potatoes.

qa.q: How did Marek feel holding up the clean potato?
qa.a: Marek felt proud, shouting "All clean!" and holding it up like a prize.

qa.q: What did Alejandro do instead of fixing the potato himself?
qa.a: He praised the scrubbing and asked Marek to find the muddy spot, so Marek could finish the job himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Alejandro to watch the splashing and the brown spot?
qa.a: Alejandro was tempted to take over, since his hand moved towards the potato, but chose patience over a quick, neat job.

grounding: Shows a young child proudly helping with a small kitchen chore, slowly and messily, and a parent who patiently accepts the imperfect help.
